Subject: GroveHealth pilot — quick sync on access corridor selection

Alice / GroveNet team —

Thanks again for the kickoff earlier. As we scope the pilot (single region, production-mirror traffic for triage routing), we need to lock the network approach. The options on the table are:

- VPC Peering (direct L3 peering)
- AWS PrivateLink / Azure Private Endpoint (endpoint-backed flows)
- Site-to-site IPsec VPN (managed by customer or partner gateway)

Key pilot goals: maintain < 40 ms p95 RTT from GroveHealth app hosts to the inference cluster, minimize rollout friction for NetOps, and avoid broad customer CIDR exposure in our control plane.

Questions for GroveNet:
1) Can you run a short traceroute from the app tier to our demo endpoint? (IP/hostname I can share once we decide).
2) Do you have any managed private connectivity partners (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute) you prefer we avoid duplicating?

Internal ask: Kim / Marcus — can you put together a brief pros/cons with the following axes: latency, operational blast radius, ease of rollback, NAT/source-IP preservation, and certs/KMS handshake constraints? I sketched a draft MOP but will wait for your input before sending to GroveNet.

Diego

Diego / team / Alice —

High-level notes below. I attached two small artifacts: an operational MOP stub (grovepilot-mop-v1.pdf) and a micro-benchmark CSV (plink-vs-peering-latency.csv) from our last pilot.

Option summary (short):

1) VPC Peering- Pros: simple L3 routing, source IP preserved (no NAT), lower per-packet overhead on provider side.- Cons: requires route table updates and potentially transitive routing issues across multiple peered VPCs; CIDR overlap blocks peering; less surface for per-service ACLs.

2) PrivateLink / Interface Endpoint- Pros: service-level abstraction, can expose only the API (no full VPC routes), easier to limit surface area via endpoint policies, compatible with customer-managed NAT.- Cons: additional hops and potential ENI-level bandwidth limits; SNAT changes source IP unless we use proxying; harder to do mutual TLS if customer insists on direct IPs.

3) Site-to-site VPN (IPsec)- Pros: quick to stand up for short pilots, broadly compatible with on-prem and cloud, simple for NetOps to control.- Cons: S2S VPN tunnels can have variable latency, limited throughput without HA tunnels, and we need an anchor IP/NAT rule on our side; exposes broader prefixes unless we implement strict ACLs.

Operational considerations:
- Zero-trust / source-auth: GroveHealth wants source-auth at the application layer (mTLS + token). Network choice does not replace app-level auth, but endpoint options reduce lateral attack surface.
- Auditability: PrivateLink endpoints produce clearer flow logs (ENI-level) vs peering (VPC flow logs aggregated).
- Rollback: With PrivateLink we can disable the endpoint; peering requires route deletions and coordination.

Recommendation for pilot: start with PrivateLink if GroveNet can accept the ENI-bound approach and we use a small proxy to preserve source metadata for logs. Fallback path: provision a temporary S2S VPN for immediate connectivity while we provision PrivateLink.

I'll add a couple of sample commands and a minimal MOP in the attached PDF.

Kim
Kimberly Park
Senior Network Architect, Redwood Inference

Thanks Kim — adding cost/latency numbers and an ops checklist. I also ran a quick synthetic from our lab (same instance type as pilot) — results are attached. Key points: 

- Latency: PrivateLink added ~6–10 ms median vs peering in-region for our sample trace, p95 delta was ~9–12 ms. VPN varied widely depending on uplink and CPU.
- Billing/ops: PrivateLink has per-ENI and data processing charges; peering has no per-flow charge but may incur transit data costs across accounts. VPN costs are low but management overhead and possible egress charges apply.
- Source IPs: If GroveHealth requires client source IP to be visible to inference nodes for rate-limiting/forensics, peering is the cleanest. PrivateLink + proxy can restore metadata but adds a hop.

Operational checklist draft:
- Baseline: run traceroute/TCP pings from app tier; verify no 172/10 CIDR overlap.
- If selecting PrivateLink:
  * Provision interface endpoint in GroveHealth account and our service network
  * Deploy a small x86 proxy pool (sidecar) to add X-Forwarded-For and sign traces
  * Validate ENI bandwidth with a 30 min soak test
- If selecting Peering:
  * Coordinate route table changes and ensure no transitive routing to third-party VPCs
  * Confirm SNAT behavior for any internet-bound flows from inference nodes
- If selecting VPN:
  * Use two tunnels (HA) with BGP offload if possible; set MTU to 1400; monitor CPU on gateways

My leaning matches Kim: start PrivateLink for least surface + fastest rollback; spin up VPN as interim if NetOps needs immediate access. If GroveHealth pushes for source-IP fidelity without a proxy, then peering.

Marcus
Marcus Lin
Infrastructure PM, Redwood Inference
